H I G H L I G H T S
• Formulate the sustainable management of a DC microgrid as a multi-reward MDP.
• Propose a multi-critic DRL framework with each reward assigned to a dedicated critic.
• Design a multi-head architecture with a shared MoE structure within the multi-critic DRL framework.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Data center microgrid Multi-critic deep reinforcement learning Mixture-of-experts Multi-reward Markov decision process
Abstract
The rapid expansion of data centers (DCs) has led to substantial increases in global energy consumption and carbon emissions. Moreover, the strong coupling among workload scheduling, IT, cooling, and energy subsystems makes sustainable DC microgrids highly complex, especially given the difficulty of accurate modeling and the presence of significant uncertainties and rapid dynamics. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a multi-critic deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach based on a mixture-of-experts (MoE) with multi-head architecture. The problem is formulated as a multi-reward Markov Decision Process (MDP) with independent reward signals for workload efficiency, energy consumption, and carbon footprint, providing richer feedback compared to traditional single-reward formulations. In the proposed approach, each reward is assigned a dedicated critic, thereby avoiding the conflicts and interference that arise when a single critic attempts to learn multiple competing rewards simultaneously. The shared MoE foundation with the multi-head architecture enables each critic head to focus on learning the value function for its specific optimization target, while the integrated adaptive gating mechanisms facilitate dynamic leveraging of both common and task-specific knowledge. This architecture improves learning stability, accelerates convergence, and enhances adaptability to complex, multi-objective learning tasks. Extensive experiments on a DC microgrid show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art DRL and rule-based baselines in reducing the overall energy consumption and carbon emissions. 1 . Introduction
1.1 . Background and motivation
Data centers (DCs) have become one of the fastest-growing sources of global energy consumption and carbon emissions in the digital revolution and artificial intelligence (AI) era. They now account for approximately 1.5% of global electricity demand and are expected to rise to 3%–4% by 2030 [1]. Correspondingly, the carbon footprint from DC electricity usage is projected to increase from around 180 Mt today to a peak of 320 Mt by 2030 [1]. In certain regions, such as the U.S., DC energy consumption could potentially reach 12% of national electricity demand as AI and cloud infrastructure continue to expand [2]. With the rapid expansion of AI and cloud services, and the growing dependence on computationally intensive technologies, the sustainable management of DCs has become an urgent priority for global decarbonization and the achievement of net-zero targets. In response, major cloud providers and DC operators (e.g., Google) aim to power their DCs with carbonfree energy 24/7 by 2030, leveraging AI-enabled workload scheduling, cooling, renewable energy, and energy storage technologies in DC microgrids [3].
